summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful in South Korea; the criminalising statute reaches only military personnel. Military Criminal Act article 92-6 penalises consensual same-sex conduct among service members with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service. Prosecutions have followed: in 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and one soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex.

The most fully documented case of state harm to a transgender person is that of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as having occurred in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available but has been conditioned by judicial guidelines the courts have since narrowed. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling required applicants to be over 20, single and without children. On 24 November 2022 an en banc panel of the Supreme Court held that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an eleven-year-old precedent that had uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors. On 8 May 2024 the Yeongdong district court declined to require sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissal of such applications; the five plaintiffs had been assigned male at birth and had been on hormone therapy for years.

South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, though registration has been contested: an NGO won before the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, the government appealed to the Seoul High Court and the Supreme Court, and Human Rights Watch described the litigation as years of bureaucratic obstruction. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records an overall relatively positive environment with free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

Health care is a documented gap. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, published in Epidemiology and Health on 27 June 2025, documented a pervasive discrimination burden across school, work and transition-related care.

Police conduct toward a transgender person has been found unlawful. The Seoul Central District Court held, in a decision final on 2 July 2024 with no appeal, that police advice to a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed her personal rights, and awarded 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

Public LGBT events have drawn organised, sometimes violent opposition. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protesters attacked participants; organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of failing to act. At Busan's 2018 Pride, some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.

Partner recognition is limited. National law recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. The Constitutional Court ruled in 2024 on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, a decision travel material treats as a landmark. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot rely on marriage or civil union for partner recognition.

Outing through state data practices is documented. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing exposed LGBTQ people's identities, and doxing and online harassment increased.
tangentialFactors:
Travel material aimed at LGBT visitors describes Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods as broadly positive for visitors, while setting that against military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition and the absence of a national anti-discrimination law.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 chapter also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and questions of assembly freedom. That turbulence concerned public gatherings and political institutions generally rather than transgender people as a group.
localsOnly:
Research presented on 20 March 2024 by DDing Dong, a youth LGBTQ+ centre, found transgender teenagers avoiding school restrooms for fear of being outed. A 16-year-old transgender girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early. The researchers called for legal and institutional reform to make school environments safer.

A 2014 study found 54% of LGBTQ South Korean youths had been harassed by classmates. Among LGBTQ people who had been outed, 16.1% were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% of those reporting harm and 94% reporting psychological trauma.

A 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults reported facing harsh discrimination in the previous year.

During the May 2020 Itaewon cluster, June Green, a transgender man working as a bartender, told NBC News he felt threatened simply walking on the street, which he attributed to the absence of a non-discrimination bill.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry on a Supreme Court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register could not be retrieved (HTTP 403). Its detail is unverified here.

No source in the inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in the civilian prison system. No birth-sex versus identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary-confinement or segregation practice is documented.

The sources do not state whether the 8 May 2024 ruling against requiring surgery for legal sex change applies beyond the case before that court.
